skills.method: The one research method the study used, named exactly (an experiment, a correlational study ...)
skills.opdef: The operational definition: how this study measured the variable, not what the concept means
skills.statistic: What a reported statistic or difference shows about these groups, with its direction
skills.ethics: An ethical safeguard the summary describes, and how the researchers applied it
skills.generalize: Whether the results generalize to a named population, from the participants' characteristics
skills.argue: A specific result used to support or refute the hypothesis, explained
skills.claim: A defensible claim that answers the question, not a topic sentence
skills.evidence: A specific, accurate result from one source, cited
skills.reasoning: How the evidence supports the claim, with a psychology concept applied (not a research word)

prompts.title: Naming the method of a twin study
prompts.context: Researchers recruited 120 pairs of identical twins and 120 pairs of fraternal twins, all raised in the same home as their twin. Every twin was 18 to 25 years old and a university student in one Northern European country. Each twin completed the same 40-item risk-taking questionnaire, scored from 0 to 160. The researchers then computed how closely the two twins in each kind of pair matched (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Identify the research method the researchers used, and explain why it fits.
checklist: Names one method: a correlational study (a twin study is a correlational design)
Explains that no variable was manipulated: twin type cannot be assigned
Does not list several methods or call the study an experiment

earns.answer: This is a correlational study. The researchers measured how strongly the twins' risk-taking scores were related within each kind of pair, and they could not assign anyone to be an identical or a fraternal twin, so nothing was manipulated.
earns.why: It names one method and ties it to the summary: the researchers measured existing pairs and manipulated nothing.

misses.answer: It is an experiment, because the researchers compared two groups: identical twins and fraternal twins.
misses.why: Two groups do not make an experiment. An experiment needs a manipulated variable and random assignment, and no one can be assigned a kind of twin.

why.1: No variable was manipulated and nobody was randomly assigned; comparing groups alone is not an experiment.
why.2: A case study looks in depth at one person or a few; this study measured 480 people on one questionnaire.
why.3: The twins filled in a questionnaire; nobody was watched in an everyday setting.

because.label: Reason
options: the researchers measured existing pairs and assigned no one to a condition
the researchers decided which twins would take more risks
the researchers studied one family in depth

why.1: Nobody was made to take risks; the researchers only measured risk-taking.
why.2: There were 240 pairs, not one family.

prompts.title: Reading twin correlations, not restating them
prompts.context: Researchers recruited 120 pairs of identical twins and 120 pairs of fraternal twins, all raised in the same home as their twin. Every twin was 18 to 25 years old and a university student in one Northern European country. Each twin completed the same 40-item risk-taking questionnaire, scored from 0 to 160. The researchers then computed how closely the two twins in each kind of pair matched (invented study for practice). Within identical pairs the scores correlated at r = .70; within fraternal pairs at r = .35.
prompts.prompt: Explain what the two correlations show about risk-taking in these twins.
checklist: Says identical twins' scores were a strong positive correlation and fraternal twins' a weak positive correlation
Says what the difference means: the more genes a pair shares, the more alike their risk-taking
Links the result to heredity (heritability) without saying genes alone cause risk-taking

earns.answer: The identical twins' scores showed a strong positive correlation (r = .70), while the fraternal twins' showed a weak positive correlation (r = .35). Identical twins share nearly all their genes and fraternal twins about half, and both kinds grew up in the same home, so the closer match in identical pairs suggests heredity contributes to risk-taking in these twins.
earns.why: It reads the numbers for the groups (stronger match for identical twins) and says what that shows (a genetic contribution), instead of copying them.

misses.answer: Identical twins had a correlation of r = .70 and fraternal twins had a correlation of r = .35.
misses.why: This only restates the numbers. A reader wants what they show: identical twins matched more closely, which points to heredity.

statistic.label: Result
options: identical twins' risk-taking scores matched more closely than fraternal twins'
fraternal twins' risk-taking scores matched more closely
both kinds of twins matched equally

why.1: That reverses the direction: .70 is the stronger correlation, and it belongs to identical twins.
why.2: .70 and .35 are not equal; the identical pairs matched more closely.

meaning.label: Meaning
options: heredity contributes to risk-taking, since identical twins share more genes
risk-taking is caused only by genes
the home environment explains the whole difference

why.1: A correlation of .70 is not 1; the result shows a contribution, not genes alone.
why.2: Both kinds of twins shared a home, so the home cannot explain why identical twins matched more.

prompts.title: Who the twin results describe
prompts.context: Researchers recruited 120 pairs of identical twins and 120 pairs of fraternal twins, all raised in the same home as their twin. Every twin was 18 to 25 years old and a university student in one Northern European country. Each twin completed the same 40-item risk-taking questionnaire, scored from 0 to 160. The researchers then computed how closely the two twins in each kind of pair matched (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Explain whether the results generalize to adults over 60 living in South America.
checklist: Takes a position: the results do not generalize (or only partly, with both sides argued)
Names participant characteristics from the summary: age 18 to 25, university students, one Northern European country
Says why those traits matter, not the sample size or the design

earns.answer: The results may not generalize to adults over 60 in South America, because every twin was an 18- to 25-year-old university student from one Northern European country. Older adults have lived through different experiences, and culture shapes how risk-taking is expressed and reported, so the link found in these young students might differ.
earns.why: It names the population, takes a position and argues from the participants' age, schooling and country.

misses.answer: No, because the study was not an experiment, so its results cannot be generalized.
misses.why: Generalizing depends on who the participants were, not on whether the study was an experiment. Name their characteristics.

claim.label: Conclusion
options: may not generalize to adults over 60 in South America

why.1: The sample was narrow; a claim about everyone ignores who was studied.
why.2: You can judge it: compare the participants with the population named.

sample.label: Participant characteristics
options: 18 to 25 years old, a university student, from one Northern European country

why.1: The number of pairs is sample size, which readers do not accept for generalizability.
why.2: The questionnaire is the measure, not a characteristic of the participants.

prompts.title: Does the drug block dopamine?
prompts.context: An animal care committee approved a study of 20 rats trained to press a lever for sugar water. Half were injected with a drug thought to block dopamine receptors and half with salt water. Rats given the drug pressed the lever 12 times a minute on average; rats given salt water pressed 30 times a minute (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: The researchers hypothesized that the drug acts as a dopamine antagonist. Explain whether the results support the hypothesis, using a specific result.
checklist: Uses a specific result: 12 versus 30 presses a minute, 18 fewer for the drug
Explains the link: an antagonist blocks receptors, so dopamine cannot pass its signal across the synapse
Takes a position (supports) without saying the study proves it

earns.answer: The results support the hypothesis. Rats given the drug pressed the lever 12 times a minute, 18 fewer than the 30 of rats given salt water. If the drug is an antagonist, it blocks dopamine receptors at the synapse, so dopamine released when the rats get sugar water cannot pass its signal, and the sugar water drives less pressing.
earns.why: It uses an accurately read result and explains how a dopamine antagonist would produce that result.

misses.answer: The results support the hypothesis because the drug is an antagonist.
misses.why: It cites no result and assumes what it should show. Use the 12 versus 30 presses and explain the link.

evidence.label: Result
options: the drug group pressed 18 fewer times a minute (12 versus 30)
the drug group pressed 18 more times a minute

why.1: That reverses the result: the drug group pressed less, 12 against 30.
why.2: They differed: 12 against 30 presses a minute.

concept.label: Explanation
options: an antagonist blocks dopamine receptors, so dopamine cannot pass its signal
an agonist mimics dopamine and strengthens its signal
a reuptake inhibitor leaves more dopamine in the synapse

why.1: An agonist would increase pressing; the drug group pressed less.
why.2: More dopamine in the synapse would increase its effect, not reduce pressing.

prompts.title: Recovering speech after surgery
prompts.context: Question: does damage to one hemisphere permanently remove the abilities it controlled? Claim: young brains can often recover abilities after one hemisphere is damaged. Source 1: 10 children had most of the left hemisphere removed before age 6 to stop severe seizures; 9 of them were using everyday speech again within two years (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Source 1 supports the claim, using a psychology concept other than neuroplasticity, the claim's own topic.
checklist: Restates the evidence briefly and cites it: 9 of 10 children regained speech (Source 1)
Applies a concept from the unit that is not the claim's own topic: hemispheric specialization (lateralization), for example
Links the concept to the claim: speech was not yet fully specialized in the left hemisphere, so the right hemisphere could take it over

earns.answer: In Source 1, 9 of 10 children regained everyday speech after most of the left hemisphere was removed before age 6. This supports the claim because of hemispheric specialization: in most adults speech depends mainly on the left hemisphere, including Broca's area, but in young children that specialization is not yet complete, so the right hemisphere could take over speech and the ability returned.
earns.why: Evidence, then a concept that is not the claim's own topic applied to these children, then the link to the claim.

misses.answer: Source 1 shows 9 of 10 children regained speech, which shows neuroplasticity, the brain's ability to change.
misses.why: Neuroplasticity is the claim's own topic, so it cannot earn the concept point, and the definition is dropped in without a link. Use a different concept and say how it let these children speak again.

why.1: Neuroplasticity is the claim's own topic, a restricted term: it cannot earn the concept point.
why.2: The all-or-none principle is about one neuron firing; it does not explain recovery after surgery.

link.label: Link to the claim
options: speech was not yet fully specialized in the left hemisphere, so the right hemisphere took it over
speech never depended on the brain

why.1: Removed tissue does not grow back; other regions take over its work.
why.2: Speech depends on the brain; that is why the surgery could affect it.

prompts.title: How this sleep study measured falling asleep
prompts.context: Forty university students spent one night in a sleep lab. Each was randomly assigned to drink either a cup of coffee with caffeine or a decaffeinated cup that tasted the same, four hours before lights-out. An EEG recorded brain activity all night. The researchers recorded the minutes from lights-out until the EEG first showed NREM sleep. An institutional review board approved the study. Each student signed an informed consent form describing the caffeine and the overnight stay, and was told they could stop and leave the lab at any time without losing the $40 payment (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Identify the operational definition of the time it took to fall asleep in this study.
checklist: Names the dependent variable: how long it took to fall asleep
Says how this study measured it: minutes from lights-out until the EEG first showed NREM sleep
Does not give a general definition of sleep or of falling asleep

earns.answer: Time to fall asleep was operationally defined as the number of minutes from lights-out until the EEG first showed NREM sleep.
earns.why: It gives the measurement this study used: a count of minutes, a starting point and the EEG sign that ended the count.

misses.answer: Falling asleep is the change from being awake into the first stage of sleep.
misses.why: That defines the concept in general. The point asks how this study measured it: minutes until the EEG showed NREM sleep.

why.1: Caffeine or decaf is what the researchers changed, the independent variable.
why.2: The payment was the same for everyone; it is not measured.

opdef.label: Operational definition
options: the minutes from lights-out until the EEG first showed NREM sleep
how tired the students said they felt
the hours each student slept the night before

why.1: The students were not asked how tired they felt; the EEG timed sleep onset.
why.2: The night before was not recorded in this summary.

prompts.title: An ethical safeguard in the sleep lab
prompts.context: Forty university students spent one night in a sleep lab. Each was randomly assigned to drink either a cup of coffee with caffeine or a decaffeinated cup that tasted the same, four hours before lights-out. An EEG recorded brain activity all night. The researchers recorded the minutes from lights-out until the EEG first showed NREM sleep. An institutional review board approved the study. Each student signed an informed consent form describing the caffeine and the overnight stay, and was told they could stop and leave the lab at any time without losing the $40 payment (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Identify one ethical guideline the summary describes and describe how the researchers applied it.
checklist: Names a guideline the summary describes: IRB approval, informed consent or the right to withdraw
Says how it was applied in this study (what the students were told or what the board did)
Does not name a design feature such as random assignment as an ethical guideline

earns.answer: The researchers respected the right to withdraw: each student was told they could stop and leave the sleep lab at any time during the night without losing the $40 payment.
earns.why: It names a safeguard the summary describes and how it was applied to these students.

misses.answer: The researchers used random assignment so the study would be fair to everyone.
misses.why: Random assignment is a design feature, not an ethical guideline. Pick a safeguard the summary describes, such as the right to withdraw.

why.1: Random assignment controls confounds; it does not protect participants.
why.2: Nobody was deceived and the summary describes no debriefing.

applied.label: How it was applied
options: students could leave the lab at any time and still get the $40
students drank coffee four hours before bed

why.1: That is the procedure, not a protection for participants.
why.2: That is the measure, not a safeguard.

prompts.title: Survey or experiment?
prompts.context: Two hundred adults in an online panel read about a surgery. A computer randomly assigned each person to one wording: "90 out of 100 patients survive" or "10 out of 100 patients die". Each person then rated how likely they would be to choose the surgery from 1 (very unlikely) to 7 (very likely) (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Identify the research method used in this study.
checklist: Names one method: an experiment
Supports it from the summary: the wording was manipulated and people were randomly assigned to it
Does not call it a survey because people answered questions

earns.answer: This is an experiment: the researchers manipulated the wording of the surgery (survive or die) and the computer randomly assigned each person to one wording before measuring their rating.
earns.why: It names one method and gives the two features that make it an experiment: a manipulated variable and random assignment.

misses.answer: It is a survey, because the participants answered a question online.
misses.why: A rating question is how the dependent variable was measured. Because the wording was manipulated and assigned at random, the method is an experiment.

why.1: The rating question is only the measure; the researchers manipulated the wording, so it is an experiment.
why.2: The researchers did not just measure two existing variables; they manipulated one.

because.label: Reason
options: the wording was manipulated and randomly assigned

why.1: Who took part does not decide the method.
why.2: The rating scale is the measure; it does not decide the method.

prompts.title: How the spacing study measured memory
prompts.context: Sixty high-school students learned 30 Spanish-English word pairs. They were randomly assigned to study in one 60-minute session or in three 20-minute sessions on three days. One week later each student saw the 30 Spanish words and wrote the English word for each (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Identify the operational definition of long-term retention in this study.
checklist: Says what was counted: the number of the 30 Spanish words translated correctly into English
Says when: on the test one week later
Does not define long-term memory in general

earns.answer: Long-term retention was the number of the 30 Spanish words, out of 30, that a student correctly translated into English on the test one week after studying.
earns.why: It gives the count, the maximum and the delay, which is how this study measured the variable.

misses.answer: Long-term retention is how well information stays in long-term memory.
misses.why: That is the concept in general. Give the measure: correct translations out of 30, one week later.

opdef.label: Operational definition
options: the number of the 30 words translated correctly
how confident students felt about the words

why.1: Confidence was not measured; the test counted correct translations.
why.2: Both groups studied for 60 minutes in all; how that time was spaced (one session or three) is the independent variable, not the measure of retention.

why.1: The summary says the test came one week later.
why.2: The summary says one week, not one month.

prompts.title: What a significant difference in recall shows
prompts.context: Sixty high-school students learned 30 Spanish-English word pairs. They were randomly assigned to study in one 60-minute session or in three 20-minute sessions on three days. One week later each student saw the 30 Spanish words and wrote the English word for each (invented study for practice). The three-session group translated 21 words on average and the one-session group 14; the difference was statistically significant (p < .05).
prompts.prompt: Explain what the statistically significant difference shows about these two groups.
checklist: Gives the direction for the groups: the three-session group recalled more, 7 more words on average
Explains significance: a difference this large is unlikely to be due to chance alone
Says what it means for spacing, without calling significance a measure of size

earns.answer: Students who studied in three shorter sessions translated 7 more words on average (21 against 14) than students who studied once. Because the difference is statistically significant, it is unlikely to be due to chance alone, which suggests that spacing study sessions improved retention for these students.
earns.why: It reads the result for the groups (direction and size) and explains what "significant" means here.

misses.answer: The three-session mean was 21 and the one-session mean was 14, and p < .05.
misses.why: It copies the numbers without saying what they show. Say which group did better and that chance is an unlikely explanation.

statistic.label: Result
options: the three-session group recalled 7 more words on average
the one-session group recalled 7 more words on average

why.1: That reverses the direction: 21 belongs to the three-session group.
why.2: 21 and 14 differ by 7 words.

meaning.label: Meaning of significance
options: the difference is unlikely to be due to chance alone
every spaced student beat every massed student

why.1: Significance is not size; it says chance is an unlikely explanation.
why.2: These are averages; significance says nothing about every single student.

prompts.title: A claim about self-quizzing
prompts.context: Question: does practicing retrieval help long-term memory more than rereading? Source 1: 120 high-school students were randomly assigned to reread a passage or to quiz themselves on it; a week later the self-quiz group recalled 62% of the ideas and the reread group 45%. Source 2: on a test five minutes after studying, both groups recalled about the same; on a test two days later, students who quizzed themselves recalled more. Source 3: in a survey of 400 students, 70% said rereading was their main way to study (invented sources for practice).
prompts.prompt: Propose a defensible claim that answers the question.
checklist: Takes a position that answers the question asked
Is a statement, not a question or a description of the topic
Can be supported or refuted with the sources

earns.answer: Practicing retrieval, such as quizzing yourself, leads to better recall on a delayed test than spending the same time rereading.
earns.why: It takes a clear position on the question that the three sources can support or refute.

misses.answer: This response will discuss retrieval practice and rereading.
misses.why: A topic sentence takes no position, so it is not a claim.

claim.label: Claim
options: practicing retrieval leads to better delayed recall than rereading

why.1: True but takes no position on the question.
why.2: A question is not a claim.

scope.label: Measure
options: only in the first five minutes

why.1: The sources measure recall, not feelings.
why.2: Source 2 found no difference at five minutes; the claim is about delayed recall.

prompts.title: Evidence, cited, from a result
prompts.context: Question: does practicing retrieval help long-term memory more than rereading? Source 1: 120 high-school students were randomly assigned to reread a passage or to quiz themselves on it; a week later the self-quiz group recalled 62% of the ideas and the reread group 45%. Source 2: on a test five minutes after studying, both groups recalled about the same; on a test two days later, students who quizzed themselves recalled more. Source 3: in a survey of 400 students, 70% said rereading was their main way to study (invented sources for practice).
prompts.prompt: Claim: practicing retrieval leads to better delayed recall than rereading. Support the claim with one piece of evidence from one source.
checklist: Gives a specific result, not a method or a participant detail
Cites the source: "(Source 1)" or "According to Source 1"
The result supports the claim

earns.answer: According to Source 1, students who quizzed themselves recalled 62% of the ideas a week later, compared with 45% for students who reread the passage.
earns.why: A specific, accurate result that supports the claim, with its source named.

misses.answer: In Source 1, 120 students were randomly assigned to either reread or quiz themselves.
misses.why: That is the method, not a result. Readers want what was found.

why.1: Source 3 reports how students study, not whether retrieval works.

evidence.label: Result
options: the self-quiz group recalled 62% a week later, against 45% for rereading

why.1: That is a method detail, not a result.
why.2: That is Source 3, and it says what students do, not what works.

prompts.title: Reasoning with a concept, not the topic word
prompts.context: Question: does practicing retrieval help long-term memory more than rereading? Source 1: 120 high-school students were randomly assigned to reread a passage or to quiz themselves on it; a week later the self-quiz group recalled 62% of the ideas and the reread group 45%. Source 2: on a test five minutes after studying, both groups recalled about the same; on a test two days later, students who quizzed themselves recalled more. Source 3: in a survey of 400 students, 70% said rereading was their main way to study (invented sources for practice).
prompts.prompt: Claim: practicing retrieval leads to better delayed recall than rereading. Evidence: Source 2. Explain how the evidence supports the claim, using a psychology concept other than retrieval practice or the testing effect.
checklist: Cites the evidence: equal recall at five minutes, more for self-quizzing two days later (Source 2)
Applies a concept from the unit that is not the prompt's topic: the forgetting curve, for example
Links it: the concept explains why the gap appeared only after two days

earns.answer: In Source 2, both groups recalled about the same five minutes after studying, but the self-quiz group recalled more two days later. This supports the claim because of the forgetting curve: most forgetting happens soon after studying, and the rereaders' recall fell away over the two days while retrieving the material slowed that drop for the self-quiz group.
earns.why: Evidence, then a concept that is not the prompt's topic, then the link that explains the delay.

misses.answer: Source 2 shows the quiz group remembered more after two days, which shows the testing effect.
misses.why: The testing effect is the prompt's own topic, so it cannot earn the concept point. Use a different concept and link it.

why.1: That is the prompt's own topic, a restricted term.
why.2: A research word never earns the concept point.

link.label: Link to the claim
options: rereaders forgot quickly over two days while retrieval slowed forgetting

why.1: Source 2 shows the rereaders' recall dropped by two days.
why.2: The summary gives no difference in study time.

prompts.title: Deception and a debriefing
prompts.context: Researchers told 90 university students the study was about attention while driving. Everyone watched the same video of a car crash at a stop sign. Half then answered questions that falsely mentioned a yield sign; half answered the same questions without it. A day later, everyone was asked which sign they had seen. Afterward the researchers debriefed each student: they explained that the study was about memory and that the yield sign had never appeared in the video (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Identify one ethical guideline the summary describes and describe how the researchers applied it.
checklist: Names debriefing (the guideline the summary describes)
Says how it was applied: the students were told the real aim and that the yield sign was never in the video
Does not name a safeguard the summary never mentions, such as confidentiality

earns.answer: The researchers debriefed the students: after the study they explained that it was really about memory and that the yield sign had never appeared, so no student left believing a false detail or the cover story.
earns.why: It names the safeguard in the summary and says how it was applied to these students.

misses.answer: The researchers kept the students' names confidential, so their answers stayed private.
misses.why: The summary never mentions confidentiality. Use a safeguard it describes: the debriefing.

why.1: The summary never describes keeping names private.
why.2: Assent is for minors; these were university students and the summary does not mention it.

applied.label: How it was applied
options: students were told the real aim and that the yield sign was false
students watched a video of a crash
half the students got misleading questions

why.1: That is the procedure, not a protection.
why.2: That is the manipulation itself; the debriefing came afterward.

prompts.title: Did the misleading question change memory?
prompts.context: Researchers told 90 university students the study was about attention while driving. Everyone watched the same video of a car crash at a stop sign. Half then answered questions that falsely mentioned a yield sign; half answered the same questions without it. A day later, everyone was asked which sign they had seen. Afterward the researchers debriefed each student: they explained that the study was about memory and that the yield sign had never appeared in the video (invented study for practice). A day later, 34% of the misled students said they had seen a yield sign, against 8% of the others.
prompts.prompt: The researchers hypothesized that misleading information given after an event changes memory of it. Explain whether the results support the hypothesis, using a specific result.
checklist: Uses a specific result: 34% against 8% reported a yield sign, 26 percentage points more
Explains the link with the misinformation effect or reconstructive memory
Takes a position (supports) without saying the study proves it

earns.answer: The results support the hypothesis: 34% of the students who got the misleading question reported a yield sign, 26 percentage points more than the 8% who did not. This fits the misinformation effect: when the students later rebuilt the memory, the false detail from the question was folded in as if they had seen it.
earns.why: It uses an accurately read result and explains how the concept produces it.

misses.answer: The results support the hypothesis, because memory is reconstructive and can change.
misses.why: A concept with no result. Use the 34% against 8% and link it to the hypothesis.

evidence.label: Result
options: 34% of the misled students reported a yield sign, against 8%
8% of the misled students reported a yield sign, against 34%
all of the misled students reported a yield sign

why.1: That reverses the groups: 34% belongs to the misled students.
why.2: Only 34% did, not all.

concept.label: Concept
options: the misinformation effect: the false detail was folded into the memory
proactive interference: an old memory blocked a new one
encoding failure: the students never saw the sign

why.1: Proactive interference is old memories disrupting new ones; here later information changed the memory.
why.2: Nobody saw a yield sign; the issue is a detail added later, not one missed.

prompts.title: The design of a vocabulary study
prompts.context: Researchers tested the vocabulary of the same 150 children at ages 2, 4 and 6, counting the words each child could name from a set of 100 pictures. They wanted to know whether children who knew many words early kept their lead (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Identify the research design and explain how you know.
checklist: Names one design: a longitudinal study
Supports it: the same children were tested at several ages
Does not call it cross-sectional because several ages appear

earns.answer: This is a longitudinal study: the researchers followed the same 150 children and tested their vocabulary at ages 2, 4 and 6.
earns.why: It names one design and the feature that defines it, the same people measured over time.

misses.answer: It is a cross-sectional study, because children of different ages were tested.
misses.why: A cross-sectional study compares different people of different ages at one time. Here the same children were retested, so it is longitudinal.

why.1: Cross-sectional compares different children of different ages at once; these are the same children retested.
why.2: There were 150 children measured the same way, not one child studied in depth.

because.label: Reason
options: the same children were tested at ages 2, 4 and 6
children of three ages took part

why.1: Several ages fit both designs; what matters is that they were the same children.
why.2: That is the measure, not the design.

prompts.title: Scoring conservation
prompts.context: Researchers tested 60 children aged 4 to 8. On each of four trials a child saw two identical glasses with the same amount of juice; then one glass was poured into a tall, thin glass. The child was asked whether the tall glass now had more, less or the same amount. A child passed if they said "the same" and explained that nothing was added or taken away, on at least 3 of the 4 trials (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Identify how this study operationally defined passing the conservation task.
checklist: Says what the child had to say: "the same"
Says what the child had to explain: nothing was added or taken away
Gives the cutoff: at least 3 of the 4 trials

earns.answer: A child passed the conservation task if, on at least 3 of the 4 pouring trials, they said the tall glass had the same amount and explained that nothing was added or taken away.
earns.why: It gives the answer, the explanation and the cutoff this study used.

misses.answer: Passing means the child understands that the amount stays the same when its shape changes.
misses.why: That defines conservation in general. Give the study's scoring rule.

why.1: "More" is the preoperational error the task looks for.
why.2: Speed was not scored; the answer and the reason were.

opdef.label: Scoring rule
options: explains nothing was added or taken away, on at least 3 of 4 trials

why.1: The cutoff in the summary is 3 of 4 trials, with a reason.
why.2: Age is a participant trait, not the scoring rule.

prompts.title: Attachment and friendship: reading r

prompts.title: Evidence that names its source
prompts.context: Question: does exercise reduce symptoms of depression? Source 1: 120 adults with major depressive disorder were randomly assigned to aerobic exercise or stretching three times a week; after 12 weeks, depression scores (0 to 60) fell 14 points for exercise and 6 for stretching. Source 2: in a survey of 3,000 adults, exercising more often was weakly related to fewer depressive symptoms. Source 3: after 16 weeks, scores fell 12 points with exercise, 13 with an antidepressant and 5 with a placebo pill (invented sources for practice).
prompts.prompt: Claim: exercise reduces symptoms of depression. Support the claim with one piece of evidence from one source.
checklist: Gives a specific result: scores fell 14 points with exercise against 6 with stretching, 8 points more
Cites the source: "(Source 1)" or "According to Source 1"
The result supports the claim

earns.answer: According to Source 1, depression scores of adults who did aerobic exercise fell 14 points after 12 weeks, 8 points more than the 6-point fall for adults who stretched.
earns.why: A specific result, cited, that supports the claim.

misses.answer: Adults who did aerobic exercise had depression scores fall 14 points, against 6 for stretching.
misses.why: Right result, but no source is named, so the evidence point is lost.

why.1: Uncited evidence loses the point.

evidence.label: Result
options: scores fell 14 points with exercise against 6 with stretching
exercise was three times a week

why.1: A participant detail, not a result.
why.2: A method detail, not a result.

prompts.title: Exercise and medication side by side
prompts.context: Question: does exercise reduce symptoms of depression? Source 1: 120 adults with major depressive disorder were randomly assigned to aerobic exercise or stretching three times a week; after 12 weeks, depression scores (0 to 60) fell 14 points for exercise and 6 for stretching. Source 2: in a survey of 3,000 adults, exercising more often was weakly related to fewer depressive symptoms. Source 3: after 16 weeks, scores fell 12 points with exercise, 13 with an antidepressant and 5 with a placebo pill (invented sources for practice).
prompts.prompt: Claim: exercise reduces symptoms of depression. Evidence: Source 3. Explain how the evidence supports the claim, using a psychology concept.
checklist: Cites the result: 12 points with exercise, 13 with an antidepressant, 5 with a placebo pill (Source 3)
Applies a concept from the unit, such as the biopsychosocial model, not a research word like placebo
Links it: a treatment acting on body and behavior can lower symptoms about as much as medication

earns.answer: In Source 3, depression scores fell 12 points with exercise, almost as much as the 13 with an antidepressant and more than the 5 with a placebo pill. This supports the claim because of the biopsychosocial model: depression involves biological, psychological and social factors, so exercise, which changes the body and daily behavior, can lower symptoms nearly as much as a medication.
earns.why: Evidence, a concept from the unit applied to it, and the link to the claim.

misses.answer: Source 3 shows exercise beat the placebo pill, so the placebo effect explains the result.
misses.why: Placebo is a research term, not the concept, and it argues against the claim.

why.1: A research term; it cannot earn the concept point.
why.2: A research term; it cannot earn the concept point.

link.label: Link to the claim
options: exercise works on body and behavior, so it lowers symptoms almost as much as medication
exercise only works as a placebo

why.1: Exercise beat the placebo pill (12 against 5 points).
why.2: The antidepressant lowered scores 13 points.

prompts.title: Music practice and math grades
prompts.context: A researcher asked 300 high-school students how many hours a week they practiced a musical instrument and collected their math grades from school records. Students who practiced more tended to have higher math grades (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Identify the research method and explain what it can and cannot conclude.
checklist: Names one method: a correlational study
Explains why: practice hours were measured, not assigned
Says it cannot show that practicing music causes higher math grades

earns.answer: This is a correlational study: the researcher measured practice hours and math grades as they were and assigned nothing, so it shows the two are related but not that practicing music raises math grades.
earns.why: One method, why it fits, and what it allows.

misses.answer: It is an experiment, because music practice is the independent variable and math grades are the dependent variable.
misses.why: Nothing was manipulated or randomly assigned; naming variables does not make a study an experiment.

why.1: Practice was not manipulated or assigned.
why.2: Students answered questions; nobody was observed.

limit.label: Conclusion it allows
options: that the two are related, not that one causes the other

why.1: A correlation cannot show cause.
why.2: It does show a relationship.

prompts.title: Questionnaires at the gym door
prompts.context: To estimate how often adults in a town exercise, a researcher handed questionnaires to 500 people as they left the town's largest gym. Respondents said they exercised 4.5 days a week on average (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Explain whether the average of 4.5 days generalizes to all adults in the town.
checklist: Takes a position: it does not generalize
Names the participant trait: every respondent was leaving a gym
Explains the bias: gym-goers likely exercise more than other adults, and the size of the sample does not fix that

earns.answer: It does not generalize to all adults in the town, because every respondent was leaving the town's largest gym. People at a gym probably exercise more than adults who never go, so the sample is biased upward, and a large sample does not fix that.
earns.why: A position argued from who the participants were.

misses.answer: Yes, because 500 people is a large sample.
misses.why: Size does not fix a biased sample. Argue from who was asked.

claim.label: Conclusion

why.2: The question asks about adults in the town.

prompts.title: Reading a negative correlation
prompts.context: A researcher surveyed 200 high-school students about how many minutes a night they used their phone after 10 p.m. and collected their grade averages. The correlation was r = −.45 (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Explain what the correlation shows about these students.
checklist: Gives direction and strength: a moderate negative correlation
Says it for these students: more phone use after 10 p.m. tended to go with lower grade averages
Does not claim phone use caused lower grades (a third variable such as sleep or workload could explain both)

earns.answer: This is a moderate negative correlation: students who used their phone more after 10 p.m. tended to have lower grade averages. It does not show that phone use lowered grades; a third variable, such as a heavy workload or poor sleep, could affect both.
earns.why: Direction and strength for these students, with the limit stated.

misses.answer: A negative correlation means phone use and grades are not related.
misses.why: Negative means one goes up as the other goes down. No relationship would be near zero.

why.1: −.45 is not near zero.
why.2: The sign is negative and .45 is moderate.

meaning.label: Meaning
options: more late phone use went with lower grades
more phone use went with higher grades

why.1: A correlation does not show cause.
why.2: That reverses the direction.

prompts.title: Which average describes the typical driver?
prompts.context: Five drivers in a simulator braked when a light came on. Their reaction times were 310, 290, 300, 1200 and 320 milliseconds; the driver with 1200 milliseconds had been looking at a phone (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Explain whether the mean or the median better describes a typical driver here.

Says the median is better because the outlier (1200) pulls the mean up
Uses the drivers: the mean is slower than four of the five

earns.answer: The median, 310 milliseconds, better describes a typical driver. The one driver who was looking at a phone took 1200 milliseconds, an outlier that pulls the mean up to 484 milliseconds, slower than four of the five drivers.
earns.why: Both values, the outlier named, and what that does to the mean.

misses.answer: The mean is 484 milliseconds, so the typical driver took 484 milliseconds to brake.

prompts.title: Two standard deviations above
prompts.context: A memory test was given to a large group of adults. Scores formed a normal curve with an average of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. Dana scored 130 (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Explain what Dana's score shows about her compared with the other adults.
checklist: Gives the z score: 2 (two standard deviations above the average)
Gives the percentile: about the 97.5th by the 68-95-99.7 rule
Says it for Dana: she scored higher than about 97.5% of the group

earns.answer: Dana's z score is 2: 130 is two standard deviations of 15 above the average of 100. By the 68-95-99.7 rule, that puts her near the 97.5th percentile, so she scored higher than about 97.5% of the adults and only about 2.5% scored higher.
earns.why: z, the percentile and what they mean for Dana.

misses.answer: Dana's z score of 2 means she scored 2 points above the average.
misses.why: z counts standard deviations, not points: 2 SD is 30 points.

why.1: That is the distance in points; z divides by the SD.
why.2: Dana is above the average, so z is positive.

why.1: 95% lies between −2 and +2; she is above all of that plus the lower tail.
why.2: 68% lies within one SD.

prompts.title: Gum and test scores
prompts.context: Sixty students were randomly assigned to chew gum or not during a 100-point vocabulary test. The gum group averaged 78 and the no-gum group 76. The difference was not statistically significant (invented study for practice).

earns.answer: The results do not support the hypothesis. The gum group scored 78 and the no-gum group 76, only 2 points higher, and the difference was not statistically significant, so it could plausibly be due to chance rather than to the gum.
earns.why: The result, what "not significant" means, and a position.
